title: Sub-Standards and Mal-Practices: Misinformation's Role in Insular, Polarized, and Toxic Interactions on Reddit
screen_reason: The paper's own question is about toxicity and polarization, not prevalence, and it prints no prevalence percentage. But it is a full-census Reddit study (Jan 2020-Jun 2021: 327M submissions, 1.6B comments, 57.2K subreddits) that reports the verbatim count of submissions hyperlinking to a domain-list of 1,054 factually unreliable news sites (633,585) alongside the verbatim total number of submissions in the same corpus (327M). That yields an exact part/whole share over the same base, which R8 permits, so one CONTENT row is kept. Everything else in the paper is toxicity/partisanship association, not prevalence.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language Reddit only, with US-based news domains and a US left-right partisanship axis (authors' stated limitation)
estimates.date: January 2020 - June 2021 (18 months, collected via Pushshift)
estimates.measure_type: % of all Reddit submissions in the study corpus that hyperlinked to a domain on a list of factually unreliable news websites
estimates.value_raw: 633,585 submission hyperlinks to unreliable news websites (stated also as 633.59K submissions) out of a final dataset of 327M Reddit submissions = 0.19%
estimates.denominator: 327M Reddit submissions - the filtered study corpus of 57.2K subreddits over January 2020-June 2021 (2.2B comments and 491M submissions collected; 18+ subreddits, non-English comments and comments outside 15-300 characters removed)
estimates.definition: A submission counted in the numerator if it hyperlinked to one of the 1,054 domains classed unreliable, i.e. rated 'Low' or 'Very Low' factuality by Media Bias/Fact Check and cross-referenced against Iffy News, OpenSources, PolitiFact, Snopes, Melissa Zimdars's list and Hanley et al. Examples given: oann.com, infowars.com, rt.com, newsmax.com, zerohedge.com, bitchute.com
estimates.misinfo_def: "we define misinformation as information that is false or inaccurate regardless of author intention. Similarly, we define unreliable domains as websites that regularly publish false information about current events and that do not engage in journalistic norms such as attributing authors and correcting errors"
estimates.source_quote: Altogether, within our set of studied 57K subreddits, we identify 633,585 submission hyperlinks to our set of unreliable news websites and a total of 7,546,917 submission hyperlinks to our set of reliable news websites.
estimates.page_loc: Numerator: p. CSCW480:11, Table 1 caption (quoted). Denominator: p. CSCW480:7, Section 3.1 - 'Altogether, our final dataset consists of 327M Reddit submissions, 1.6B comments, and 15.5M users from 57.2K subreddits.'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Media Bias/Fact Check factuality ratings, dichotomised (Low or Very Low = unreliable; Mostly Factual, High or Very High = reliable), giving 1,054 unreliable and 3,754 reliable domains, cross-referenced against Iffy News, OpenSources, PolitiFact, Snopes, Melissa Zimdars's list and Hanley et al. No human coding, so no inter-rater reliability applies
estimates.moderator_quote: We study 18 months of Reddit comments and submissions from January 2020 to June 2021, which we collected using Pushshift [14]. [...] Altogether, our final dataset consists of 327M Reddit submissions, 1.6B comments, and 15.5M users from 57.2K subreddits.
estimates.notes: DERIVED VALUE - flag for adjudication. The paper never prints a prevalence percentage; the share is an exact part/whole from two verbatim counts over the same corpus, which R8 permits, but the counts come from two different sections and the denominator (327M) is rounded to three significant figures, so 0.19% is precise only to that rounding. Interpretation matters: the denominator is ALL Reddit submissions of any kind (links, images, text posts), not news submissions, hence denom_scope=all_media - this is the platform-wide item-level prevalence of unreliable-news links, directly comparable to platform-wide Facebook/Twitter figures, and it is NOT the share of news links that are unreliable (see missed_or_uncertain). Domain-level proxy: falsity is attributed by publisher, never assessed per item, so breadth is left blank per the source-level rule and the authors themselves flag that this 'inevitably missed some subtleties of unreliable information'. The paper's own qualitative summary agrees with the direction of this number: 'its overall prevalence compared to reliable news sources is low' and 'unreliable websites have much less of a presence on Reddit compared to reliable websites'.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) SHARE OF NEWS-LINK SUBMISSIONS that are unreliable - 633,585 vs 7,546,917 reliable links would give about 7.8%, but that denominator has to be built by SUMMING two categories, which R8 explicitly forbids ('NEVER keep a cross-category sum'). This is the number most readers would want and it is not licensed. (2) COMMENT-LEVEL / engagement-weighted version: 'we find 633.59K submissions of unreliable news websites and a corresponding set of 5.29 million comments; we further find 7.55 million submissions that link to our set of reliable websites and 267 million corresponding comments', against the corpus total of 1.6B comments. 5.29M/1.6B = 0.33% of all Reddit comments were posted under an unreliable-domain submission. This is derivable the same way as the row above (part/whole, same corpus) and an adjudicator may want it as a SHARING/engagement-weighted row; I left it out under R4 (one derived estimate I am confident in beats two), and because a comment under a link is engagement with, not itself, unreliable content. (3) CONCENTRATION: no row is possible under R1. The paper asserts concentration only qualitatively ('unreliable information is largely concentrated within a few communities on Reddit') and attributes it to another paper; Table 1 gives the top-10 subreddits' unreliable-link counts, but converting them to a share of the 633,585 total would require summing ten cells (a cross-category sum). Also NOT usable: the Weld et al. figure quoted in the literature review ('over 99% of extremely biased and low factual content hyperlinks were shared in only 0.5% of Reddit communities') - a figure cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8. (4) Subreddit-level coverage: hyperlinks to unreliable websites appeared in 9,462 subreddits and reliable in 29,673 (8,611 in both) out of 57.2K - a share of COMMUNITIES containing at least one unreliable link (about 16.5%), which fits no construct in the schema (it is not user-level REACH) and is not extracted. (5) All toxicity figures (1.26% of all comments toxic; 1.24% under reliable vs 1.55% under unreliable submissions; the 25%/32% relative increases; 2.01% vs 1.40% subreddit toxicity) measure toxicity, not misinformation. (6) Homophily figures (71.80% of interactions same-partisanship overall, 83% under unreliable submissions, 66% under reliable; 72.08%/80.63%/63.34% of toxic interactions) are interaction composition, not misinformation prevalence. (7) Per-domain intensity (601 submissions per unreliable domain vs 2,010.4 per reliable domain) is a mean count, not a share of anything the review measures. (8) Alexa reach of the lists (991 reliable domains, 26.39%, vs 139 unreliable, 13.19%, in the top 100K sites) describes the domain lists themselves. (9) Throwaway-account figures (2.64% of unreliable vs 0.88% of reliable submissions posted in an account's first week) and moderation figures (2.01% vs 2.82% comments removed; 16.74% vs 16.26% moderator involvement) have unreliable/reliable submissions as denominators and are not falsity shares.

rob.design: Full-census observational platform study, no human participants and no human coding. 18 months of Reddit (January 2020-June 2021) collected via Pushshift before it left Reddit's ToS: 2.2B comments and 491M submissions raw, filtered to 327M submissions, 1.6B comments, 15.5M users and 57.2K subreddits by excluding 18+ subreddits, non-English comments and comments outside 15-300 characters. Unreliability assigned at the domain level from Media Bias/Fact Check factuality ratings dichotomised into 1,054 unreliable and 3,754 reliable domains, cross-referenced against six additional published lists; no item-level or claim-level verification, so no inter-rater reliability statistic exists or applies. Toxicity from the Google Jigsaw Perspective API SEVERE_TOXICITY classifier at a 0.80 threshold (authors note this favours precision over recall); subreddit/user partisanship and politicalness from Waller et al.'s Word2Vec embedding method, validated by a 0.828 Pearson correlation with Waller's published subreddit partisanship scores. Toxicity norms computed only for subreddits with at least 100 comments and users with at least 5 comments, skewing to active communities. AutoModerator and labelled bot accounts removed from the analyses. Author-stated limitations: domain-level proxy misses subtler misinformation, English and US-centric only, activity threshold skew, residual confounding and no causal claim, and the data predate ChatGPT.
rob.item6_quote: As in previous studies [7, 62, 65, 78, 85, 102, 162], we define misinformation as information that is false or inaccurate regardless of author intention. Similarly, we define unreliable domains as websites that regularly publish false information about current events and that do not engage in journalistic norms such as attributing authors and correcting errors [3, 7, 28, 65, 75, 116, 140, 171].
rob.item10_quote: Altogether, within our set of studied 57K subreddits, we identify 633,585 submission hyperlinks to our set of unreliable news websites and a total of 7,546,917 submission hyperlinks to our set of reliable news websites.
